Neonates of Southern reef squid emerge from eggs measuring between 5 and 10 mm in diameter and possess a wet weight at birth of only 0.22 g [Wwb = 0.22 g]. This minimal initial mass, typical of many loliginid hatchlings, reflects the limited yolk reserves packaged into each egg and constrains the early life stages to a brief period of endogenous nutrition before the onset of active planktotrophic feeding. In laboratory rearing trials conducted at a stable temperature of 28 °C [T = 28 °C], females attained a maximum lifespan of 305 days [am = 305 days], a relatively short longevity that is consistent with the rapid, semelparous life history documented in related tropical and subtropical squid species. Under these same thermal conditions, cumulative reproductive output at the moment of death for females reached approximately 380 oocytes , indicating a substantial lifetime investment in egg production that is tightly concentrated into the terminal phase of the adult stage at a temperature of 28 °C [T = 28 °C]. The interplay between hatchling size and adult reproductive allocation appears to be a key axis of life-history variation within the Sepioteuthis genus.

Sexual maturation in Southern reef squid follows a markedly dimorphic pattern with respect to body size. Females typically initiate gonadal development at a mantle length of 7 cm [Lp = 7 cm], a comparatively small size that suggests an early commitment to reproductive physiology relative to somatic growth. Males, by contrast, delay the onset of puberty until they reach a mantle length of 15 cm [Lp = 15 cm], a threshold that likely reflects the elevated energetic demands associated with male-male competition and the production of large spermatophores. This divergence in size at maturation between the sexes is a recurring theme among loliginids and is thought to be driven by sexual selection pressures that favour larger body size in males during agonistic encounters over access to receptive females. Field surveys of wild populations have confirmed that mantle length at the time of first functional gamete production reliably distinguishes the two sexes, making it a practical metric for assessing population reproductive status and for parameterising demographic models used in fisheries management.

The lifespan and reproductive schedule of female Southern reef squid are tightly coupled to ambient water temperature, as demonstrated by controlled laboratory experiments. When held at a constant temperature of 28 °C [T = 28 °C], females lived for a maximum of 305 days [am = 305 days], a duration that aligns with the upper range of values reported for other tropical cephalopods reared under similar thermal regimes. This relatively compressed lifespan, combined with the observation that cumulative oocyte production at death amounted to 380 oocytes  under the same thermal conditions, suggests that females channel available resources almost exclusively into a single, massive reproductive effort rather than spreading investment across multiple prolonged spawning seasons at a temperature of 28 °C [T = 28 °C]. In cooler waters typical of the southern Australian range, where seasonal temperatures can drop well below this experimental benchmark, both growth rates and longevity are expected to shift, potentially altering the timing of maturation and the total fecundity achieved before senescence.

Comparative data on mantle length at death reveal a consistent pattern of sexual size dimorphism in this species. Females were recorded with a terminal mantle length of 45 cm [Li = 45 cm], a size that appears to represent a physiological optimum balancing the costs of somatic maintenance against the benefits of increased egg-carrying capacity. Males, in contrast, reached a longer final mantle length of 55 cm [Li = 55 cm], a divergence that is frequently interpreted as a consequence of intrasexual competition for mating opportunities favouring larger body size among males. This difference of 10 cm in terminal mantle length between the sexes is substantial relative to overall body size and has direct implications for the interpretation of catch data in the commercial trawl fishery that targets this species along the coasts of Queensland and New South Wales. The ecological drivers maintaining this dimorphism likely include differential predation risk, as larger individuals may face reduced vulnerability to gape-limited predators, and differential energetic returns from foraging at larger body sizes.

The reproductive biology of Southern reef squid is characterised by a terminal investment strategy in which females die shortly after completing egg deposition. Under laboratory conditions maintained at 28 °C [T = 28 °C], the total number of oocytes produced over a female's lifetime reached 380 (380 oocytes) , a value that represents the cumulative reproductive output at death. This substantial fecundity, achieved despite a maximum lifespan of 305 days [am = 305 days] under the same thermal regime, underscores the intensity of reproductive effort that defines the species' life history at a temperature of 28 °C [T = 28 °C]. Males, with their larger terminal body size of 55 cm [Li = 55 cm] mantle length compared to 45 cm [Li = 45 cm] in females, experience a different selective landscape; the size at puberty for males is 15 cm [Lp = 15 cm], double the 7 cm [Lp = 7 cm] threshold observed in females, a pattern that reinforces the interpretation that delayed maturation in males allows the attainment of a competitive advantage in the mating system.
